title: How do geckos walk on ceilings?
hook: No glue, no suction cups: the secret is in impossibly fine hairs.
summary: A gecko’s toes carry millions of microscopic hairs that split into even tinier tips and cling through a weak attraction between molecules, the van der Waals force.
cardText: Millions of microscopic hairs on its toes, each splitting into hundreds of tiny tips, get so close to the surface that a weak pull between molecules holds the gecko up. No glue, no suction.

cardBlocks.text: Slide your finger across clean glass and it skids. A gecko’s toe doesn’t. Under its toes sit millions of microscopic hairs called setae, and each seta branches at its tip into hundreds of even smaller pads called spatulae, which look like broccoli under a microscope.

Those tips get so close to a surface that a feeble attraction between the molecules of the foot and those of the wall starts to matter: the van der Waals force. On its own it is negligible; added up over billions of spatulae, it holds the animal upside down. Researchers ruled out the alternatives: the feet have no glue glands, suction would be far too weak, and geckos stick even in a vacuum.
Geckos cling because billions of microscopic tips touch the wall so closely that the pull between molecules adds up to plenty of grip.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Sticking is easy; letting go is the hard part

A running gecko has to attach and release each foot 15 times a second. The trick is the angle: tilt a seta up to about 30 degrees and its spatulae let go easily. So the gecko simply peels its toes off the surface, the way you would peel off tape.

In 2000, researchers measured the force of a single seta for the first time, in a study in Nature on the tokay gecko, a species from Southeast Asia. By the team’s estimate, one hair could lift an ant, and a million of them, covering an area the size of a dime, could lift a child of about 20 kilograms. On glass in the lab, a gecko may need no more than 10% of its setae to hold on.

In 2000 the authors still could not rule out that a thin film of water helped. In 2002, new tests showed that gecko toes stick equally well to surfaces that repel water and to surfaces that attract it, which pointed to van der Waals forces. A neat consequence: what matters is the size and shape of the tips, more than the chemistry of the wall.
The idea has inspired dry adhesive tapes made of carbon nanotubes that mimic setae and spatulae. Not every surface works, though: geckos cannot stick to Teflon.
